27279:
Deborah is the only judge in the book who is also called a prophet, and the only one described as already judging before the crisis. Israelites came to her under her palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim to have disputes settled. When Jabin of Hazor and his commander Sisera, with nine hundred iron chariots, had oppressed Israel for twenty years, she summoned Barak with God's command. She went with him to battle when he insisted and foretold that a woman would get the glory.

The victory at the Kishon is told twice, in prose (Judges 4) and in poetry (Judges 5). The Song of Deborah is widely regarded as one of the oldest compositions in the Bible. It credits the victory to the LORD marching from Seir and to a storm that turned the plain into mud, and it praises the tribes who volunteered while shaming those who did not. Deborah calls herself 'a mother in Israel'.

Her role has been central in debates about women's leadership in church and synagogue. Some see her as clear precedent for women in authority. Others see her as an exceptional case at a time when men failed to lead. Both sides agree that the text presents her positively and with no hint of disapproval.
27280: She was a prophetess, the wife (or 'woman') of Lappidoth, and judged Israel under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. She summoned Barak, accompanied him to Kedesh and Tabor, foretold Sisera's death at a woman's hand, gave the signal for battle, and sang the victory song with Barak. The land rested forty years.
27281: The Talmud counts Deborah among the seven prophetesses of Israel (b. Megillah 14a). Some rabbis criticise her for self-praise in the Song ('until I arose') and say her prophecy briefly left her as a result. The Targum presents her as a teacher of Torah.
27283: Deborah exercised prophetic, judicial and national leadership with God's evident approval. This shows that God calls women to lead, and her example supports women's ordination and leadership.
27285: Deborah's leadership is genuine and honoured, but some argue it is presented as exceptional. She hands military command to Barak, delivers God's word rather than her own authority, and her story exposes male hesitancy (Judg 4:9). On this view it is not a pattern for church eldership, which the New Testament addresses separately.
27286: She is honoured as a holy prophetess and read as a type of the Church or of Mary, the woman through whom the enemy is defeated.
27287: The Song (Judg 5) is often dated to the 12th–11th centuries BC and is a key source for early Israel's tribal structure. The prose account is regarded as a later retelling with some differences, for example in which tribes take part.
27290: Courage to go to the battlefield
27291: Gives the glory to God in song
27292: None recorded in the text (some rabbinic commentators fault the self-reference in her song)
27294: The day of battle at Tabor
27296: In the Iron I period the central highlands were held by Israelite villages, while Canaanite city-states such as Hazor and Megiddo controlled the valleys with chariot forces. The Jezreel Valley and the Kishon river formed the battlefield. Heavy rain could flood the Kishon and bog down chariots, which fits the poem's 'stars fought from heaven'. Tribal levies were voluntary, which explains the song's praise and blame of different tribes.
27297: Her name became a symbol of women's wisdom and courage in Jewish and Christian history. The Song of Deborah is studied as a masterpiece of Hebrew poetry and a key witness to early Israel. Her story is the most frequently cited Old Testament example in debates on women in ministry.
27298: Deborah is one of the seven prophetesses of Israel (Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah and Esther).
27299: Authoritative and poetic, motherly yet commanding. She speaks in vivid imagery and with confident certainty about God's word.

The Song of Deborah calls her 'blessed above women'. Her act broke the expected customs of hospitality and her clan's peace with Jabin, and interpreters have long debated whether she was a heroine of faith or a troubling figure of deception.
27329: She went out to meet Sisera, invited him in, gave him milk, covered him, and killed him with a tent peg and hammer. The song blesses her above women in the tent.

27331: Some Fathers read her as a type of the Church crushing the enemy's head (compare Gen 3:15). Others are troubled by the breach of hospitality and limit the praise to her siding with God's people.

27369:
Gideon of the clan of Abiezer in Manasseh was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from Midianite raiders when the angel of the LORD called him a mighty man of valour. A reluctant hero, he asked for repeated signs, among them the famous fleece. Yet he pulled down his own family's Baal altar and, with an army that God cut from 32,000 to 300, routed the Midianite hordes in a night attack with trumpets, jars and torches.

The second half of his story darkens. He takes harsh revenge on the towns of Succoth and Penuel, executes the Midianite kings in a blood feud for his brothers, and makes a golden ephod that becomes an object of idolatrous worship. He refuses the crown in words ('the LORD shall rule over you'), yet he lives like a king with many wives and seventy sons, and he names one son Abimelech, 'my father is king'. That son's bloody grab for power follows his death.

The book of Judges uses Gideon as a hinge. Before him the judges improve Israel. From him on, the deliverers themselves increasingly reflect Israel's decline. Isaiah remembers 'the day of Midian' as a model of God's decisive deliverance, and Hebrews lists Gideon among those who by faith 'out of weakness were made strong'.
27370: He was son of Joash the Abiezrite and was called by the angel of the LORD. He destroyed Baal's altar, was clothed by the Spirit, and tested God with a fleece. With 300 men he defeated Midian, pursued and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and punished Succoth and Penuel. He declined kingship, made an ephod that became a snare, had many wives and seventy sons, and died in a good old age after forty years of rest.
27371: The rabbis debate his merit. Some count him among the three least of the judges who were nonetheless as great in their generation as Moses, Aaron and Samuel in theirs (b. Rosh Hashanah 25b). His ephod is generally condemned.
27372: The Fathers read the dew on the fleece as an image of the Incarnation and of Mary's virginal conception (the fleece wet while the ground is dry). This reading is reflected in hymnody.
27374: Gideon shows God's strength made perfect in weakness, since the 300 make clear that the victory is the LORD's. Many caution against using 'putting out a fleece' as a normal way to discern God's will, since it began in his doubt. His later decline warns that early faith can end in spiritual compromise.
27376: Scholars note the irony of Gideon's refusal of kingship. Some read Judg 8:23 as genuine anti-monarchic theology, while others read it as a polite formula undercut by his royal lifestyle. The Gideon–Abimelech cycle is seen as Judges' extended reflection on kingship before Samuel.
27377: Obedient in destroying idolatry despite fear
27378: Trusted God with a tiny army
27381: Harsh vengeance on Succoth and Penuel
27382: The ephod that became an idol
27383: A royal lifestyle that prepared for Abimelech's tyranny
27387: The offer of kingship and the ephod
27388: Midianite, Amalekite and 'eastern' camel-riding raiders swept seasonally into the Jezreel Valley to plunder harvests. This is one of the earliest biblical portrayals of domesticated camels in warfare. Threshing in a winepress, a sunken vat, was a way of hiding grain. Ephods could be priestly garments or cult objects for seeking oracles.
27389: 'The sword of the LORD and of Gideon' became a rallying cry. The Gideons International, founded in 1899 and known for distributing Bibles, took his name from his willing small band. 'Putting out a fleece' entered common speech. Isaiah and Psalm 83 recall the defeat of Midian as a model of divine rescue.
27390: The dew on Gideon's fleece is a figure of the incarnation in the Virgin's womb.
27391: Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit* 1 (prologue); Christian liturgical tradition

He argued Israel's claim to the land with a detailed appeal to history, received the Spirit, and won. But his rash vow ended in tragedy for his only daughter, and his quarrel with Ephraim ended in a massacre at the Jordan fords. Whether he actually sacrificed his daughter or dedicated her to lifelong virginity is a long-standing debate. Hebrews still lists him among those who acted by faith.

Recalled from Tob, he negotiated with Ammon, received the Spirit, vowed a burnt offering, defeated Ammon, and 'did with her according to his vow' to his daughter, whose fate became an annual lament. He fought Ephraim and judged six years.

27418: The 'and' of Judg 11:31 can be read 'or'. The emphasis on her virginity and the annual lament suggest she was devoted to perpetual celibate service at the sanctuary, since human sacrifice was forbidden (Deut 12:31). Defenders argue this better explains Hebrews 11:32.

27453:
Samson is the last and most paradoxical of the major judges. His birth was announced by an angel, he was consecrated a Nazirite from the womb, and the Spirit of the LORD repeatedly rushed upon him with superhuman strength. Yet he was driven by appetite and revenge, chasing Philistine women, breaking his Nazirite separation (touching a carcass, holding a drinking feast), and finally giving away the secret of his consecration to Delilah.

His exploits are private feuds rather than national campaigns. He never raises an army, and the men of Judah would rather hand him over than fight (Judg 15:11-13). Still, the text insists that God was at work through his choices to 'begin' Israel's deliverance from the Philistines (Judg 13:5; 14:4). Blinded and enslaved, he prays for the first time for himself and God, and in his death he brings down Dagon's temple.

Readers have long been divided. Some see a tragic hero whose final prayer of faith is honoured in Hebrews 11. Others see a mirror of Israel itself: set apart by God, compromised by assimilation, and finally humbled into dependence. Some critical scholars detect folk-hero or solar-myth motifs in his name and deeds, while others defend the stories as rooted in early Israelite–Philistine border conflict.
27454: The text says he was son of Manoah of Zorah, a Danite, and a Nazirite from birth by angelic command. He married a Timnite woman, killed a lion, posed a riddle, and killed Philistines at Ashkelon, Lehi and elsewhere. He judged Israel twenty years. He told Delilah his secret, was shaved, blinded and imprisoned, and died bringing down the temple of Dagon in Gaza. The Spirit is named as the source of his strength, and the LORD's departure as the reason he lost it.
27455: The rabbis are ambivalent. They note that he 'went after his eyes' and so lost his eyes (Mishnah, *Sotah* 1:8), yet they count him a true judge. Some read Jacob's blessing of Dan, 'a serpent by the way', as a prophecy of Samson (b. Sotah 10a).
27456: Many Fathers read Samson as a type of Christ, whose birth was announced by an angel, who was betrayed for silver, and who defeated his enemies in his death with arms outstretched. Augustine defends his death as obedience to a hidden divine command rather than suicide (*City of God* 1.21).
27457: Samson shows God's sovereign grace working through deeply flawed people (Judg 14:4) and the danger of treating God's gifts casually. Hebrews 11:32 honours not his morals but his final dependence on God.
